exam.title: CSE120 Midterm Exam
exam.description: Midterm covering operating system fundamentals: synchronization, deadlock, scheduling, exceptions, threads, and join behavior in Nachos.
exam.instructions: Select the best answer for each question. You have 80 minutes to complete this exam.

questions.question_text: 1(a) Does the test-and-set instruction need to be a privileged instruction?
questions.explanation: Test-and-set does not need to be privileged because the hardware can safely allow user-level execution of atomic read-modify-write operations.

questions.question_text: 1(b) What approach to dealing with deadlock does the Banker's algorithm implement?
questions.explanation: The Banker’s algorithm checks whether granting a resource request is safe. This allows the OS to avoid entering unsafe states that may lead to deadlock.

questions.question_text: 1(c) Which of the following scheduling algorithms can lead to starvation? FIFO, Shortest Job First, Priority, Round Robin
questions.explanation: Shortest Job First favors shorter jobs and may starve long ones; Priority scheduling may indefinitely delay low-priority tasks if high-priority tasks continue arriving.

questions.question_text: 1(d) A program containing a race condition will always/sometimes/never result in incorrect behavior?
questions.explanation: Race conditions do not always manifest; the result depends on timing. A program may behave correctly during some executions even if a race exists.

questions.question_text: 1(e) A system meeting the four deadlock conditions will always/sometimes/never deadlock?
questions.explanation: The presence of the four deadlock conditions enables deadlock but does not guarantee it. Deadlock may or may not occur depending on resource requests.

questions.question_text: 2(a) Categorize: Timer — interrupt, exception, or neither?
questions.explanation: A timer event is generated asynchronously by hardware and is therefore an interrupt.

questions.question_text: 2(b) Categorize: Segmentation violation — interrupt, exception, or neither?
questions.explanation: Segmentation violations occur synchronously as a result of illegal memory access and therefore are exceptions.

questions.question_text: 2(c) Categorize: Keyboard input — interrupt, exception, or neither?
questions.explanation: Keyboard input is an asynchronous hardware event that generates an interrupt.

questions.question_text: 2(d) Categorize: Divide by zero — interrupt, exception, or neither?
questions.explanation: Divide-by-zero faults occur synchronously due to program behavior, making them exceptions.

questions.question_text: 2(e) Categorize: Procedure call — interrupt, exception, or neither?
questions.explanation: A procedure call is a normal control-flow transition and neither an interrupt nor an exception.

questions.question_text: 2(f) Categorize: System call — interrupt, exception, or neither?
questions.explanation: System calls trap into the OS via a synchronous software exception.

questions.question_text: 3. Discuss the tradeoffs between user and kernel threads. What are the advantages and disadvantages of each?
questions.correct_answer: User threads have fast switching but no true parallelism; kernel threads are slower but fully scheduled by the OS and can run in parallel.
questions.explanation: User threads avoid kernel involvement, so creation and switching are fast, but all threads in a process block if one makes a blocking system call. Kernel threads are managed by the OS, allowing independent scheduling and parallelism, but incur overhead for context switching and creation.

questions.question_text: 3(b) If system calls were as fast as procedure calls, would one thread model be preferable?
questions.explanation: If the main drawback of kernel threads—the cost of kernel transitions—disappears, their advantages (parallelism, independent scheduling) dominate.

questions.question_text: 4(a) Give an execution sequence where two cars travel in opposite directions on the bridge simultaneously using the unsynchronized code.
questions.correct_answer: North thread passes check then context switches; south thread also passes check; both increment num_cars and enter.
questions.explanation: Each thread checks the condition before num_cars is incremented. If both reach A.0 before either increments num_cars, both enter despite opposite directions.

questions.question_text: 4(b) Show how to correctly annotate the code using Lock and Condition.
questions.correct_answer: Use a lock around checks and updates; cars wait on cv until direction is open or matches their own; broadcast when num_cars reaches zero.
questions.explanation: Correct solution uses lock->Acquire(), cv->Wait(lock), and cv->Broadcast(lock) ensuring mutual exclusion and proper wakeup behavior.

questions.question_text: 4(c) Indicate which lines form critical sections.
questions.correct_answer: A.-1 to A.3 and D.-1 to D.5.
questions.explanation: All modifications of num_cars and cur_dir must be atomic and therefore belong in critical sections.

questions.question_text: 4(d) Can this solution lead to starvation?
questions.explanation: If cars continuously arrive in one direction, cars in the opposite direction may wait forever.

questions.question_text: 4(e) Can this solution lead to deadlock?
questions.explanation: There is no circular wait—cars going opposite directions cannot block simultaneously.

questions.question_text: 5(a) What does the test program print under round-robin scheduling with no priorities?
questions.correct_answer: fee foe foo far fie fum fun
questions.explanation: Main prints 'fee foe'; A prints 'foo far'; B prints 'fie'; A prints 'fum'; main prints 'fun'. This sequence follows FIFO and blocking semantics.

questions.question_text: 5(b) What does the test program print when threads are scheduled using priorities?
questions.correct_answer: fee foo fie far fum foe fun
questions.explanation: High-priority A and B preempt the main thread after creation. Output reflects immediate execution of higher priority threads.
